messages.author: fb40a65bd21dcf6f
messages.subject: Missing data in matrix
parts:
Hi,

I have a matrix of counts which I want to model as below but I would like to hold out some of the counts to test the out-of-sample behaviour of my model. As I understand it Stan should work more efficiently when everything is vectorized but that isn't so easy to do in my case as the rate parameter for each matrix entry is the product of a column rate and a row rate. I was hoping to use an approach where the likelihood for the whole matrix is modelled and then increment_log_prob() is called with the inverse probability for the held-out data. Maybe this is a crazy thing to do but I figured at the end of the day I was just adding and subtracting from the log probability. When I tried it, it failed to converge (Rhat was way off 1). Is it possible to do this sort of thing or do I need to rearrange my data into vectors and also have index vectors to know which columns and rows each data is from? I hope the code below makes it clearer what I'm trying to do:
                                               
data {
    int<lower=1> N;
    int<lower=1> M;
    int<lower=0> counts[N,M];
    int<lower=0> heldout[N];  // Index of held out datum for each row
}
parameters {
    vector<lower=0>[M] colsizes;                                                                  
    vector<lower=0>[N] rowrates;
}
model {
    vector[M] rates;
    colsizes ~ lognormal(0, 1);
    rowrates ~ lognormal(2, 3);
    for (n in 1:N) {                                              
        rates <- rowrates[n] * colsizes;
        counts[n] ~ poisson(rates);
        # Add back the held out data
        increment_log_prob(-poisson_log(counts[heldout[n]],
                                        rates[heldout[n]]));
    }
}

parts: OK it seems like I had a bug in the code (nothing new there then).

increment_log_prob(-poisson_log(counts[heldout[n]],
                                        rates[heldout[n]]));

should be

        increment_log_prob(-poisson_log(counts[n, heldout[n]],
                                        rates[heldout[n]]));

Sorry for the noise but any comments on whether this technique is worthwhile from an efficiency standpoint would be welcome.

Regards,
John.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix

On Sep 29, 2014, at 6:25 AM, John Reid <johnba...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> I have a matrix of counts which I want to model as below but I would like to hold out some of the counts to test the out-of-sample behaviour of my model. As I understand it Stan should work more efficiently when everything is vectorized but that isn't so easy to do in my case as the rate parameter for each matrix entry is the product of a column rate and a row rate. I was hoping to use an approach where the likelihood for the whole matrix is modelled and then increment_log_prob() is called with the inverse probability for the held-out data. Maybe this is a crazy thing to do but I figured at the end of the day I was just adding and subtracting from the log probability. When I tried it, it failed to converge (Rhat was way off 1). Is it possible to do this sort of thing or do I need to rearrange my data into vectors and also have index vectors to know which columns and rows each data is from? I hope the code below makes it clearer what I'm trying to do:
>
> data {
> int<lower=1> N;
> int<lower=1> M;
> int<lower=0> counts[N,M];
> int<lower=0> heldout[N]; // Index of held out datum for each row
> }
> parameters {
> vector<lower=0>[M] colsizes;
> vector<lower=0>[N] rowrates;
> }
> model {
> vector[M] rates;
> colsizes ~ lognormal(0, 1);
> rowrates ~ lognormal(2, 3);
> for (n in 1:N) {
> rates <- rowrates[n] * colsizes;
> counts[n] ~ poisson(rates);
> # Add back the held out data
> increment_log_prob(-poisson_log(counts[heldout[n]],
> rates[heldout[n]]));
> }
> }

I don't understand why there's a negation of the log probability
for the "held out" data.

If you really want to calculate the held out probability, you
can do that in the generated quantities block, e.g.,

generated quantities {
real heldout;
for (n in 1:N)

heldout <- heldout
+ poisson_log(counts[n,heldout[n]], rates[heldout[n]]);
}

Then heldout should be the held out data's log probabilty in the model
and there's no connection back to fitting.

But you'll need to redefine rates in terms of the parameters, or
move its definition into transformed parameters (but that will save it).
The recomputation in generated quantities is relatively fast because
there are no gradient calculations.

This doesn't do anything like the "cut" in BUGS --- you still
get connectivity in the model between the "held out" data and
the estimates of rowrates and colsizes.

It also looks like you have a multiplicative identifiability issue
in that you can multiply colsizes by C and divide rowrates by C and
get the same model. The priors may be enough, but you should be careful
with this.

- Bob

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix
parts:
Just to clarify, I believe Bob and John are thinking about two different ways to hold out data for out-of-sample predictive validity (correct me if I'm wrong):

Bob: hold out a data point by putting it in a separate container in the data block and fit the model to the rest of the data; then evaluate the held-out data point in the generate quantities block.

John: just put all the data in a single container and negate the log probability of single data point (while also including it in the sampling statement for all the data) such that it effectively doesn't contribute to the posterior and the model is fitted to anything but that data point.

Bob's approach is cleaner and more efficient because it avoids unnecessary calculations. Further it avoids the risk of non-perfect negation due to differences in numerical stability between increment_log_prob() and sampling statements (if that is actually possible in Stan - probably not).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix
parts:
John,

I don't know what platform you are using, but if you work in R (like me), pre-processing your data should be easy to automate. You would probably have to let go of your current matrix format and provide the data to the model along with two dummy integer arrays that identify the original positions in the matrix (if you absolutely need that). You can then do your outer product by looping through the data vector, using the dummy vector as indexes for your parameters. And then at the end, you only need one sampling statement, rather than N.

Dropping an item from the data vector (and the corresponding items from the integer arrays) during pre-processing of data should be no problem at all.

Luc

parts:
Just in case we're still not on the same page, I'm suggesting the following:

data {
  int<lower=1> N;           // number of observations to which you are fitting the model
  int<lower=1> N_out;    // number of out-of-sample observations to which the model is not fit
  int<lower=1> P;           // number of rows in the original data matrix
  int<lower=1> Q;          // number of columns in the original data matrix

  int<lower=0> counts[N];                            // observed counts to which the model is fit
  int<lower=1,upper=P> row_index[N];        // row indices for data to which the model is fit
  int<lower=1,upper=Q> col_index[N];         // column indices for data to which the model is fit

  int<lower=0> counts_out[N_out];                            // out-of-sample observed counts to which the model is not fit
  int<lower=1,upper=P> row_index_out[N_out];        // row indices for out-of-sample data to which the model is not fit
  int<lower=1,upper=Q> col_index_out[N_out];         // column indices for out-of-sample data to which the model is not fit 
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> rowrates[P];
  real<lower=0> colrates[Q];
}
model {
  real rates[N];

  colrates[N] ~ lognormal(...);
  rowrates[M] ~ lognormal(...);
for (n in 1:N)

rates[n] <- rowrates[row_index[n]] * colrates[col_index[n]];
 
  counts ~ poisson(rates);
}
generated quantities {
  real rates_out[N_out];
 
  for (n in 1:N_out)
    rates_out[n] <- rowrates[row_index_out[n]] * colrates[col_index_out[n]];
 
  // Whatever magic you need to do with parameter "rates_out" and data "counts_out"

}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Missing data in matrix
parts:
On Sep 30, 2014, at 12:24 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Isn't this the same as how an outer product works in the inner bowls of Stan? I guess it all boils down to that, as the efficiency gain from a fully vectorized sampling statement will be quite small as there are no shared components between the elements of counts (each is modeled by a different rate). Bob?

Correct. I wouldn't expect to see much difference in performance from
vectorizing a Poisson that has a different rate for each count being modeled.
Vectorizing will eliminate a bunch of virtual function calls under the
hood, but in our measurements, those don't seem to take up much time (prefetch
seems pretty darn good when there's no branch prediction to go wrong).

But where you will save time is in not doing unnecessary log probability
calculations in the model that could be done in the generated
quantities block. The reason is that we calculate gradients for everything
in the model and that's the main bottleneck in Stan's processing.
So anything to reduce the number of gradients or process them faster is
a win. The generated quantities block just works on values (double in C++),
which are a lot faster to calculate.

- Bob
